title: Non-Markovian Quantum Dynamics of Exciton-Polaritons
authors: Rajanya Sarkar, Pritha Ghosh, Arshath Manjalingal, David R. Reichman, Arkajit Mandal
abstract: Exciton-polaritons, hybrid light-matter quasiparticles formed when a material interacts with a confined electric field, have experimentally been shown to exhibit mesoscale coherent quantum propagation that remains robust at room temperature. However, an accurate and direct quantum dynamical simulation of this phenomenon that does not resort to semi-classical approximations is prohibitively expensive computationally, limiting the microscopic understanding of the rich dynamical interplay among phonons, photons, and electrons under collective light-matter coupling. To address this fundamental challenge, we develop a non-Markovian master equation approach which enables the fully quantum mechanical simulation of non-equilibrium exciton-polariton dynamics and captures phonon-induced decoherence and dissipation beyond the conventional Markovian limit. To carry out this task, a procedure is developed in which the wave vector space is coarse-grained and each diagonal element of the density matrix is evolved in parallel. To demonstrate the utility of this approach, we simulate exciton-polariton transport in TIPS-pentacene. We find that our approach reasonably captures the experimentally observed renormalization of the polariton group velocity, which originates from the phonon-induced non-Markovian Lamb shift. We further show that this renormalization cannot be reproduced within conventional Markovian theories.
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of simulating exciton-polariton dynamics quantum mechanically by developing a non-Markovian master equation approach. By employing advanced computational techniques like time-local propagation and k-space coarse-graining, the authors accurately model phonon-induced decoherence. The key finding is that only the non-Markovian treatment can reproduce the experimentally observed renormalization of the polariton group velocity.
main_problem: Developing an accurate, fully quantum mechanical simulation of non-equilibrium exciton-polariton dynamics that avoids computationally prohibitive methods and semi-classical approximations.
main_result: The non-Markovian approach successfully captures the experimentally observed renormalization of the polariton group velocity, a feature that conventional Markovian theories fail to reproduce.
method: The authors employ a non-Markovian Nakajima-Zwanzig master equation, solved using a time-local propagation scheme combined with coarse-graining of the wave vector space.
model_or_system: The system involves exciton-polaritons (hybrid light-matter quasiparticles) coupled to a phonon bath, modeled using a generalized Holstein-Tavis-Cummings Hamiltonian. The dynamics are simulated in the lower-polariton subspace.
key_observables: Exciton-polariton group velocity renormalization, phonon-induced decoherence (purity), and polaritonic density evolution.
important_parameters: Phonon coupling strength, time scale (sub-picosecond), and the distinction between Markovian and non-Markovian regimes.
main_assumptions: The memory kernel is treated to second order in the polariton-phonon coupling, and the wave vector space is coarse-grained using a three-tiered approach.
figures_summary: Figures compare group velocities from non-Markovian simulations against various Markovian approaches and experimental data, showing clear discrepancies. Snapshots illustrate density evolution under different theoretical treatments.
paper_structure: The paper develops the non-Markovian master equation, addresses computational scaling issues via time-local propagation and k-space coarse-graining, and then applies this framework to simulate polariton transport, comparing results against established Markovian limits.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses open quantum system dynamics in solid-state light-matter systems, providing a rigorous quantum mechanical tool to study decoherence and transport beyond the standard Markovian assumptions common in quantum optics.
